The Rake stardrum (Stellifer rastrifer) is a demersal sciaenid species inhabiting the coastal waters of the southwestern Atlantic, where its life-history strategy reflects the energetic constraints of a warm-temperate estuary. Field surveys conducted along the Brazilian coast have documented that females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 126 grams [Wwi = 126 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to a large sample of adult individuals. In contrast, the wet weight at birth for this species is exceedingly low, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing just 0.00053 grams [Wwb = 0.00053 grams], a figure consistent with the small egg diameter of approximately 1 millimeter that characterizes many batch-spawning sciaenids. This minimal neonatal mass places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum for its family, demanding a rapid transition to exogenous feeding following yolk-sac resorption. Juvenile recruitment into the estuarine nursery grounds appears closely tied to the onset of the rainy season, which enhances planktonic productivity and prey availability for the early larval stages.

The onset of sexual maturation in Stellifer rastrifer occurs at a relatively modest size compared to the species' ultimate dimensions. More specifically, the total length at puberty has been established at 9.8 centimeters [Lp = 9.8 centimeters] based on histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected across multiple annual cycles. This length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty for females of approximately 9.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 9.6 grams], a mass that represents a substantial investment in somatic growth before the allocation of resources toward reproductive effort begins. The transition to maturity is marked by the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, leading to the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Individuals below this size threshold are almost exclusively immature, highlighting a sharp ontogenetic boundary between the juvenile and adult phases of the life cycle.

Reproductive output in the Rake stardrum is characterized by a protracted spawning season that coincides with elevated water temperatures typical of the austral summer. Females are batch spawners, releasing individual clutches of approximately 74 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 74 eggs per spawning event], with an average of approximately one spawning event per day [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per day] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C]. This high-frequency, low-fecundity strategy is typical of sciaenids that produce numerous small, pelagic eggs over an extended breeding period. The daily reproductive rate implied by these two parameters is substantial, reflecting a life history that prioritizes iteroparity and repeated spawning over the production of a single, large clutch. Such a strategy buffers against stochastic mortality events during the planktonic larval phase, a period of extreme vulnerability for the species.

The maximum recorded longevity for Stellifer rastrifer is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] when examined in populations from the warmer portions of its geographic range at a temperature of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C]. This lifespan estimate, derived from otolith-based age determinations of wild-caught specimens, was obtained under the prevailing thermal regime of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C] that characterizes its estuarine habitats. This relatively extended lifespan, compared to other small-bodied sciaenids, allows for multiple reproductive seasons and a cumulative lifetime fecundity that compensates for high early-life mortality. Senescence in this species is gradual, with older individuals exhibiting reduced condition factors and lower gonadosomatic indices before eventual post-reproductive mortality. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 32.1 centimeters [Li = 32.1 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to the oldest age classes within the population and is among the larger records within the genus Stellifer.

Comparative analyses within the Sciaenidae family reveal that Stellifer rastrifer occupies an intermediate position on the fast-slow life-history continuum, balancing a moderate lifespan with a high reproductive output. Unlike some short-lived congeners that complete their life cycles in less than two years, this species delays first reproduction until the second year of life, allowing individuals to approach the total length at puberty of 9.8 centimeters [Lp = 9.8 centimeters] before initiating their first spawning event. This prolonged juvenile phase ensures that females reach a body size capable of supporting the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and repeated spawning across multiple seasons. The extremely small wet weight at birth of 0.00053 grams [Wwb = 0.00053 grams] necessitates a planktonic larval phase characterized by rapid growth and high metabolic rates, dependent upon the warm, productive waters of the estuary. The combined life-history traits of moderate size, extended reproductive window, and high fecundity per unit time enable this species to maintain stable populations despite the environmental variability inherent to its coastal habitat.
